articles.title: A 45-year-old refinery worker from Chelmsford, Essex used ChatGPT to answer every letter in a three-year fight over a £100 Newquay parking fine that rose to about £300, and the company dropped the case before court
articles.summary: A Chelmsford refinery worker successfully eliminates a £100 parking fine, escalating to £300 over three years, aided by ChatGPT. Discover how AI helped him navigate the complex dispute with a car park operator.
articles.body: A 45-year-old refinery worker from Chelmsford, Essex, has had a £100 parking fine cancelled after spending three years challenging the penalty with help from ChatGPT. The charge, issued after he paid for parking 16 minutes after entering a car park in Cornwall, had increased to around £300 before the company withdrew its case ahead of a scheduled court hearing.Rafal Goral received the penalty from Smart Parking Limited after visiting Tower Road car park in Newquay on August 4, 2023. He disputed the charge, saying a long queue at the payment machine and problems with card payments had forced him to use a mobile app instead, according to The Independent.Rather than pay the fine, Goral continued challenging it through correspondence with the parking operator and debt collection agencies. Throughout the process, he uploaded letters and emails to ChatGPT and used its responses to prepare replies and understand the steps involved in contesting the charge.The dispute ended in his favour in September this year, when Smart Parking informed him that the case and penalty had been dropped. Goral said the outcome was about standing by his position rather than avoiding the payment.“From start to finish it was not about the money, I could pay it, but it is about the principle,” he said.“If you know you are right then you shouldn’t be paying any money to them.”How a 16-minute delay led to a three-year parking disputeGoral arrived at Tower Road car park at around 10.12am on August 4, 2023, during a visit to Newquay. He joined a queue at the pay-and-display machine but said it was accepting cash only when he reached the front, According to The Independent.He then downloaded the RingGo app and created an account to complete the payment. Poor mobile signal added to the delay, meaning he paid 16 minutes after entering the car park.Smart Parking issued a parking charge notice on August 25, 2023, citing insufficient parking time as the reason for the penalty. The initial charge was £100.Goral appealed in September, but said he received no response before a debt collection agency contacted him in January with a demand for £170.He said he spent the following four months corresponding with the agency before the matter was placed on hold. After that, he heard nothing for around 18 months.The dispute resurfaced in November last year when another debt collection company contacted him. Goral was subsequently informed that the matter was due to go to court in October 2026, prompting him to prepare a defence.He also said Smart Parking had offered to reduce the charge to £60 through a mediation process, but he rejected the proposal.How ChatGPT helped prepare his defenceGoral said he relied on ChatGPT throughout the dispute, uploading each letter and email he received and asking the AI chatbot how to respond. He also used it to prepare a defence that he submitted to the court ahead of the scheduled hearing.“I did it all with the help of AI. They even prepared my defence which I sent to the court,” he said.He also contacted Citizens Advice several times but felt the guidance he received from the organisation was less useful than the assistance provided by the chatbot.The parking company withdrew the case on September 25, just weeks before the scheduled hearing. By then, Goral said the amount being pursued had risen to approximately £300.Reflecting on the outcome, he described the cancellation as a major relief after years of correspondence and uncertainty.“I was so ready to go to court. I would have gone all the way to the high courts,” he told Sell Us Your Story.“I won the war without the final battle.”Goral also urged other motorists to challenge parking penalties they believe have been issued incorrectly, rather than paying simply to avoid dealing with a lengthy dispute.“People don’t want to go through the hassle, so they just pay but it is wrong. It is shocking,” he said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation
articles.summary: The actress said how stressful" it was with people "talking about you... in ways you can't comprehend".
articles.body:
Florence Pugh has said she was "disturbed" to see "thousands of people" discussing her recent appearance at the Governors Awards, and denied speculation about weight-loss drugs and facial surgery.

The actress wrote on Instagram how "stressful" it was waking up to people "talking about you and your body in ways that you can't even comprehend".

"I have never been on Ozempic. I have never done any face surgery," she wrote. "And don't ever say that I didn't make my own nose, I've always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby!"

She added: "For the first time in my entire career, I have had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily."

In her eight-page statement, the Oppenheimer, Dune and East of Eden star told followers: "I'm looking after myself, and that's literally it."

Pugh highlighted that losing weight had not been her goal, and she had lost "two pounds".

"The thing that's most important to me and my trainer is muscle," she said. "I think it's the most important thing a woman can do. Build muscle and be strong. I can now do six pull-ups and lift 110kg.

"Which I'm sure to many of you isn't a lot... but to me?! It's everything."

The actress said that from the moment she entered the acting industry she was "subjected to fat shaming".

"I have loved every time I get to tell someone they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I'm not changing that now just because you've all said so."

She also said she was "disturbed" that "women who now think that I'm someone I'm not, for having my body dissected and pointed at again".

"I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow."

Professor Heather Widdows from Everyday Lookism , which campaigns to end body shaming, told BBC News: "Pugh is right that we are in a place where 'beauty standards are changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with'.

"A global beauty ideal makes impossible demands and normalises what were once extreme," added Widdows, who is Professor of Philosophy at the University of Warwick.

"We know that body-shaming individuals is harmful. Given this, we should not say negative things about other people's bodies... in a world where our bodies are increasingly ourselves, when you shame bodies you shame people."

Pugh, who was Oscar-nominated for Little Women in 2020 and played Black Widow assassin Yelena Belova in this year's Spider-Man: Brand New Day, has previously spoken out against judgement about women's looks.

In 2024, she told the Times she aimed to "challenge how women were perceived".

"Look, not everybody has legs that go on for days. I remember watching this industry and feeling that I wasn't represented," she said. "I've loved challenging ideas I don't like."

She also spoke about why she thinks she receives criticism about her appearance.

"I've always been aware that seeing a confident woman be happy in her skin is triggering to a lot of people and for a long time just accepted that I will receive commentary like that," she said.

"But now this...? I'm asking us all to just be mindful. We are real people, living real lives."

Pugh did not have comments turned on for her post, but it was liked by celebrities including Ashley James, who is known for speaking out about body positivity, plus Carol Vorderman, Zoe Ball, writer and actress Katy Brand and doctor and broadcaster Amir Khan.

Pugh also said she had sued several publications earlier this year, claiming they published AI-generated images appearing to show her receiving cosmetic injections that were presented as real photographs.

"I was... horrified," she wrote, claiming the articles had damaged her reputation.

The actress concluded by urging followers to think about their attitudes towards physical appearance.

"I understand that we are in a warped part of image history right now, with beauty standards changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with," she said.

"But please be gentle to yourselves and others when you go in on people's physical appearance.

"I'm not angry at you, I'm angry at the situation that's being projected onto us.

"It feels inescapable, but part of changing the tide is on you as much as us in the public eye."

articles.title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'
articles.summary: Early efforts to contain coronavirus "were doomed to fail", the public inquiry has found. Here's what you need to know.
articles.body:
Early efforts to contain coronavirus "were doomed to fail" because the test, trace and isolate system in the UK could only handle a relatively small number of cases, the seventh report of the Covid inquiry says in a damning assessment.

Across 245 pages the inquiry looks at everything from border controls to how well contact tracing worked.

UK blind to how quickly Covid was spreading

The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.

Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.

NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.

In the end, more than £30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.

But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.

It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.

Inquiry chair Baroness Hallett said the UK should have been better prepared and learnt lessons from other countries that had experience of dealing with outbreaks of other infectious diseases, such as Sars.

Unlike the UK, places such as Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had established systems ready to go.

This was despite the fact the UK had run a series of simulation exercises in the years leading up to Covid.

They included Exercise Cygnus into a flu pandemic and Exercise Alice into Mers. Both identified problems relating to test, trace or isolation, which appear not to have been fully acted on.

The report also raises the question of whether the government could have made use of non-government testing facilities in hospitals, universities and the private sector from the start, instead of just relying on 12 government labs.

When people in the UK were told to isolate, "many felt forgotten and let down by the lack of practical or financial support when trying to follow the rules", says the report.

In the early months of the pandemic, estimates suggested less than half of people were complying with the rules around isolating if infected.

Ministers and their advisers discussed this and fines of up to £10,000 were introduced for those who did not comply, which some experts have said was counter-productive.

Changes were made to allow people to claim statutory sick pay.

But it was not until September in England – and later in Scotland and Wales – that £500 financial payments were introduced to help those on low incomes comply.

More also needed to be done to provide practical support for things such as collecting medicines and shopping for food for those who did not have people to call on.

Suspending all flights from China to the UK in February 2020 could "have provided valuable additional time to prepare healthcare systems for the impact of the pandemic", said inquiry chair Baroness Hallett. That didn't happen.

The report says the UK lacked a clear strategy for implementing border control measures early in the pandemic, which left the country in an "extremely vulnerable position".

Although the closure and restriction of borders was noted as "immensely complex", the inquiry said that border control measures could serve as an important tool "to reassure the public and increase confidence."

By April 2020, 93% of countries had put measures in place, such as flight suspensions, border closures and travel restrictions, to control their international borders.

By contrast, the UK government only requested travellers arriving from high-risk areas to self-isolate for 14 days. The UK government implemented no further border control measures until June 2020.

The report says that border controls were a "critical gap in the UK's ability to limit the spread of the virus" and recommends that in the future "international border control measures should be in place at the earliest stages of a pandemic".

The inquiry report is more positive about the use of smartphone apps, saying digital tools can have a "significant impact on reducing the spread of infection".

It quotes a mathematical modelling study from the US which estimates that, when 75% of people used a contact tracing app in the pandemic, infections were reduced by at least 50%.

Three different apps were developed during Covid - one for England and Wales, another for Scotland and a third for Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.

The inquiry says that took up "valuable time", and it recommends developing a UK-wide digital tool to use in any future outbreak.

It says it is "fundamentally important" that apps and digital tools are as accurate as possible – and people have confidence in them.

In the summer of 2021, as Covid restrictions were relaxed, around 7% of all UK adults were told to self-isolate over a seven-day period, something dubbed by the press as the "pingdemic".

It quotes Treasury estimates suggesting that may have reduced economic growth by as much as 0.3% that month.

articles.title: A BC condo owner who said her neighbours’ scented laundry kept her off her balcony since 2018 has lost her case, after a tribunal ruled laundry smells come from a reasonable, lawful everyday activity
articles.summary: A BC condo owner has lost her legal battle against neighbors over scented laundry smells, with a tribunal ruling these odors are part of everyday life that residents must tolerate.
articles.body: A condominium owner in British Columbia, Canada, has lost a legal complaint against her neighbours over scented laundry products after a tribunal ruled that the smell from washing and drying clothes was part of an ordinary household activity that residents must tolerate.The woman had argued that fragrances from neighbouring apartments created an “overwhelming stench”, preventing her from opening her windows or spending time on her balcony. She wanted the strata council to enforce its nuisance bylaw and require residents to stop using scented laundry products.However, the province's Civil Resolution Tribunal dismissed her claim, finding that the source of the odours could not be established and that the use of laundry fragrances did not amount to an unreasonable interference with other residents, according to CTV News.In a decision, tribunal member Alissa Reynolds noted that although the woman said the problem had affected her since 2018, the first formal complaint was recorded in 2023.Strata council investigated complaints over laundry smellsThe strata council, which oversees the condominium's common property and shared facilities, formed a committee to investigate the woman's concerns.According to the tribunal decision, the investigation involved identifying dryer vents close to her apartment, visiting neighbouring units and asking residents to stop using and dispose of scented products. The council also circulated a notice to the entire complex requesting that occupants avoid such products.Despite these measures, the woman continued to report the smell.Reynolds said the council could not establish where the odour was coming from after eliminating the nearest dryer vents as possible sources.“I find it is not possible for the (strata council) to identify the ongoing source of (the woman’s) complaints, given it has now eliminated the closest dryer vents,” she wrote.The tribunal also considered the possibility that the smell originated beyond the condominium complex. Reynolds pointed out that the property was situated in a densely populated neighbourhood surrounded by other apartment buildings and businesses.“The (complex) is located in a densely populated community with several neighbouring apartment buildings and businesses, and the scent could be coming from outside the (complex),” the decision stated.Tribunal says laundry fragrances do not amount to a nuisanceThe woman also submitted a physician's letter confirming that she had multiple chemical sensitivities. She described the laundry odours as “terrible fumes” and argued that they affected her ability to use her home comfortably.However, Reynolds found that the evidence did not establish that fragrances coming specifically from neighbouring dryer vents posed a health risk to the complainant.The tribunal also examined whether the alleged interference met the legal threshold for a nuisance under the strata's rules. According to the decision, the test requires an activity to cause an unreasonable, continuing or repeated disruption to another resident's use and enjoyment of their property. The impact must also be substantial rather than minor.Even if the source of the smell had been identified, Reynolds concluded that the use of scented laundry products would not breach the nuisance bylaw.“I find laundry scents are the result of a reasonable and lawful activity and ordinary citizens must tolerate a minor degree of neighbourhood loss of amenity or slight annoyance,” she wrote.The tribunal member added that a reasonable person would not consider the reported interference substantial or non-trivial.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kemi Badenoch defends amputee marathon runners claim in benefits cut row
articles.summary: Paralympian Richard Whitehead had accused the Conservative leader of "weaponising" his sporting success.
articles.body:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has defended her suggestion that because double amputees run marathons more disabled people should work instead of claiming benefits.

Her comments were criticised by Paralympian Richard Whitehead, who accused her of "weaponising" his sporting success, while Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the Tory leader's words "crass and insensitive".

But in an interview with the BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Badenoch stood by the remarks, insisting that "if people even with significant problems can work, then those who have ADHD and mild anxiety should go to work".

Asked if she accepted the comments were insensitive, Badenoch said: "No, no, no. I do not accept it. I will speak the truth, and I will say what I believe is common sense. I will speak the truth, and I will say what I believe is common sense.

"What I know is that if people can work, then we should encourage them to work."

Badenoch acknowledged she had used "extreme examples to illustrate things", but added: "If someone can do that, then yes, your condition of ADHD or anxiety is mild."

"I will say things as they are. People may disagree with things that I say, and that's fine, this is a free country, people are free to disagree, but they know where I'm coming from," she said.

"I start from first principles: If you can work, you should work, and the Conservative Party is going to help you get a job."

Government backs welfare shake-up to prevent 'lost generation'

What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending?

In a speech setting out the Conservative Party's welfare plans last week, Badenoch said: "The reality is that millions of people can and do contribute to our economy, to their families, to their communities even when they face serious challenges.

"Double amputees run marathons. People who are housebound do wonderful creative work from home. People with autism run some of the biggest tech companies in the world."

Responding to her speech, Whitehead - a double amputee marathon runner who has won four Paralympic medals - said he was "gobsmacked that somebody's sporting success would be weaponised in this way" .

In a post on social media , he also said: "Disability should never be judged through isolated examples of individual achievement, but through an understanding of the barriers people and families face every day.

"The fact that some double-leg amputees can run marathons does not mean that disability support is unnecessary.

"Equally, the fact that some people with ADHD thrive despite limited support does not mean that others do not need meaningful assistance."

As part of their plans to cut welfare spending, the Conservatives have proposed stopping people from claiming disability benefits for "milder mental health issues and neurodiversity conditions such as anxiety, depression and ADHD", as well as "routine back and joint pain".

The party says its proposals to overhaul sickness and disability benefits would save £13.7bn a year.

It would also invest £1bn into health support, so people no longer eligible for cash benefits can access treatment to support their conditions instead.

articles.title: Mrima Hill deal: US consortium wins Kenya mining project, beating Chinese rivals
articles.summary: The Mrima Hill site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (£45bn).
articles.body:
A US-led consortium, Frontier Minerals, has won the tender to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill mining project, beating seven bidders, including companies from China and Australia.

The site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (£45bn), including niobium, used in electric vehicles, aerospace and defence technology.

Frontier Minerals says its proposal aims to keep more of the economic benefits in Kenya through "processing and refining of minerals in-country".

The deal comes as Washington seeks greater access to Africa's minerals, aiming to strengthen US supply chains and compete with China.

Frontier Minerals brings together three US companies - Bunker Hill Mining Corp, American Resources Corporation and ReElement Technologies Corporation. The consortium combines expertise in mineral resource development, critical materials supply chains and advanced refining technologies.

A central part of its proposal is to develop mineral processing and refining capacity in Kenya. Brad Barnett from Frontier Minerals said the company wanted the country to capture more value from its mineral resources.

Mrima Hill is located in Kwale County, near Kenya's Indian Ocean coastline. The site covers about 390 acres of forest.

The prospect of mining in the area has raised concerns among local residents, who fear the project could damage the forest and threaten their ancestral heritage.

There are also questions over whether communities living near the site will benefit from the investment.

Barnett was keen to reassure Kenyans that they would benefit: "We intend to create lasting opportunities for Kenyan workers, businesses and the wider economy through capacity-building and targeted investment, while prioritising environmental management and performance."

The consortium must still obtain a prospecting licence and meet the necessary regulatory requirements before the project can proceed.

The tender decision has drawn objections from competing bidders.

Reuters news agency reports that two rival companies intend to challenge the selection, with Australia's RareX alleging that Frontier Minerals missed an earlier submission deadline.

Kenya's government has maintained that the process was open and transparent.

The project comes as US strives to secure alternative sources of critical minerals and reduce dependence on China, which dominates the processing of several key minerals.

Washington has been pursuing partnerships with mineral-rich African countries, including the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, as it seeks to strengthen supply chains for industries ranging from electric vehicles to defence technology.

Kenya's mining ministry says the sector is an important part of its plans to diversify the economy beyond traditional sources of revenue such as tourism, agriculture and financial services.

A man has been jailed for five months after causing an estimated £10,000 worth of damage to Belfast's Big Fish sculpture.

Peter Smith, 44, of no fixed abode, admitted criminal damage and possessing items with intent to damage property.

He is believed to have used a hatchet, a hammer and a sledgehammer to smash ceramic tiles around the sculpture's left eye.

District Judge Francis Rafferty told Belfast Magistrates' Court: "I regard it as a targeted attack, but it remains unexplained."

Police were called to Donegall Quay shortly after midnight on 20 September. A witness saw Smith striking the sculpture with a long-handled object and detained him until officers arrived.

Smith was carrying a hammer and a small hatchet in his backpack and officers later found a sledgehammer in nearby bushes.

Defence barrister Garrett O'Kane said Smith was visiting Belfast from England and that he had a psychiatric disorder following a car crash four years earlier in which two of his sons were killed.

O'Kane said Smith told him that he had found the tools and used them to attack the sculpture.

The court heard that plans for repairing the sculpture remain unclear.

articles.title: Bloomberg reporter barred from Trump-Xi-Putin meeting after question on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
articles.summary: A Bloomberg reporter, Annmarie Hordern, was barred from covering a key diplomatic meeting between President Trump, President Xi, and President Putin after asking about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's loyalty to the U.S. The incident raises concerns about media access during international engagements.
articles.body: A Bloomberg reporter was prevented from covering the opening remarks of a meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin after asking Trump about former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang during an earlier bilateral meeting with Xi.Annmarie Hordern was excluded from the press group covering the trilateral meeting on Thursday because she had raised the question during Trump's earlier discussion with the Chinese president, according to a White House press pool report.The report said White House officials attempted to have the journalist reinstated, but Chinese representatives insisted she remain excluded.“A Bloomberg reporter was barred from this spray because she asked a question during the bilateral meeting with Xi,” the pool report stated.The White House attempted to have Hordern reinstated, but Chinese officials reportedly refused to allow her back into the meeting.During the earlier meeting, Hordern had asked Trump whether Huang had been disloyal to the United States. Trump did not respond to the question.The incident highlighted restrictions on journalists' access during diplomatic engagements in China. In the United States, reporters routinely ask questions during on-camera meetings between the president and foreign leaders.Trump also commented on media access during his visit, saying earlier on Thursday: “It's too bad the media couldn't see some of it, because every move was perfectly executed.”The three leaders discussed United Nations reform, oil production and supply, the International Criminal Court and the threat of nuclear conflict, according to statements released by Russia and China.Why was Jensen Huang at the centre of the question?The question about Huang came amid controversy surrounding his personal relationships and allegations involving a Singapore-based businesswoman, Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials reportedly suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence.According to reports, the relationship may have helped Singapore-based company Megaspeed secure Nvidia chips despite US export restrictions on China, raising concerns over possible national security implications.Huang acknowledged infidelity, while Nvidia's board launched an independent investigation into the matter and said it had no reason to believe confidential information had been compromised.Huang resigned on November 12, 2026, with chief financial officer Colette Kress taking over as interim CEO.Huang has said he would return to the company if asked, although the board appears opposed to the possibility.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Rhode Island mansion built in 1901 for about $1.4 million is reopening with a new multisensory museum experience, turning a Gilded Age summer estate into an interactive journey through its past
articles.summary: A historic Rhode Island mansion that once hosted the wealthy during America’s Gilded Age has opened its doors to visitors with an unusual new attraction.
articles.body: A historic Rhode Island mansion that once hosted the wealthy during America’s Gilded Age has opened its doors to visitors with an unusual new attraction. The Elms, a Newport estate completed in 1901, is now home to an immersive museum experience that combines film, sound, storytelling and fragrances to recreate life inside the grand residence more than a century ago. According to the Preservation Society of Newport County, which operates the property, the project was developed with Emmy-winning creative studio Digital Kitchen. Local broadcaster Ocean State Media also reported on the experience following its opening on November 16, 2026. Scroll down to read more.A historic mansion gets an immersive makeoverCalled The Elms Experience, the new attraction aims to take visitors beyond traditional house tours by allowing them to experience the mansion through multiple senses. Rather than simply observing period furniture, artwork and architecture, guests encounter carefully designed installations that recreate aspects of everyday life in the early 20th century. The experience unfolds across 20 rooms, incorporating video projections, soundscapes, character dialogue, physical displays and specially developed scents. The installations are designed to bring the stories of the people who lived and worked at the estate into focus, including the wealthy family, their guests and the household staff.Some of the details are particularly unusual. Ocean State Media reported that visitors entering the Green Room encounter an orange-inspired fragrance, while projections of monkeys associated with the Berwind family appear in the Butler’s Pantry. The Dining Room, meanwhile, features a table arranged for a dinner party of 12, offering a glimpse into the elaborate social gatherings that once took place inside the residence.The project was developed over nearly three years, with Digital Kitchen working alongside the Preservation Society’s curatorial team. The storytelling draws on historical research into the mansion’s occupants, architecture, collections and domestic life.The story behind The ElmsThe Elms was commissioned by Edward Julius Berwind, a businessman who built his fortune in the coal industry, and his wife, Herminie. The couple used the property as their summer residence, reflecting the extraordinary wealth and European-influenced tastes associated with Newport’s Gilded Age elite.Completed in 1901 at a reported cost of approximately $1.4 million, the mansion was designed by architect Horace Trumbauer. Its architecture was inspired by Château d’Asnières, an 18th-century French residence outside Paris. The interiors and furnishings were created by Allard et Fils, whose work helped give the house its distinctly European character. The property also became home to an impressive collection of Italian Renaissance ceramics, 18th-century French artwork, 17th-century Venetian paintings and Chinese jades.After Berwind’s death in 1936, his sister Julia continued spending summers at the estate until her death in 1961. The Preservation Society of Newport County acquired the property in 1962 and subsequently opened it to the public. The Elms was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1996.Blending technology with preservationDespite its use of modern technology, the new experience has been designed to respect the mansion’s historic interiors and architecture. The Preservation Society said the project followed the US Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for the Treatment of Historic Properties, with research and conservation guiding the installation process.Visitors can also use a mobile companion accessible through QR codes placed throughout the property. It provides additional historical information, educational material and references to the research behind the installations, allowing guests to explore the mansion’s history beyond the physical tour.The project is supported by BankNewport as its founding partner. The Preservation Society describes the initiative as an effort to make historic house museums more engaging for contemporary audiences while maintaining their educational and preservation responsibilities. The Elms Experience opened to the public on November 16, 2026, with special timed admission tickets. The mansion is part of Newport Mansions, a collection of 11 historic properties managed by the Preservation Society of Newport County.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Peace talks over, business mode on: Trump unveils $17 billion Asia deals
articles.summary: After wrapping up his high-profile 'Big Three' meeting focused on peace, Donald Trump was back to business, quite literally.
articles.body: After wrapping up his high-profile 'Big Three' meeting focused on peace, Donald Trump was back to business, quite literally.The US president has unveiled a $17 billion package of deals across Southeast Asia, spanning Boeing aircraft, HIMARS rocket systems, energy projects and artificial intelligence investments.According to a White House fact sheet released on Wednesday, the package includes commercial agreements, defence purchases and investment commitments involving the Philippines, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei.The administration said the deals would support tens of thousands of American jobs while expanding US economic and strategic ties across Southeast Asia.Philippines accounts for the biggest chunkThe Philippines emerged as the biggest beneficiary of the announced package, with a $12 billion deal for 20 Boeing 787 aircraft for Philippine Airlines, finalised with Boeing and GE Aerospace. The agreement is expected to support around 47,000 American jobs, according to the White House.Washington and Manila will also pursue a defence financing package worth more than $2 billion to facilitate Philippine purchases of American military equipment.In a separate commitment, the US will provide $400 million in military financing to strengthen the Philippines' capabilities in the South China Sea, including long-range fires, command and control systems, infrastructure and multi-domain drones.Beyond defence and aviation, the Philippines has also secured several technology and infrastructure commitments. These include a $37 million contract for AI-enabled military mission support, a separate $63 million initiative to modernise defence cloud infrastructure and a potential $200 million satellite connectivity deal with US company Astranis.The two countries will also explore cooperation on civil nuclear technology, while projects worth $40 million for a fuel storage depot at Subic Bay and the modernisation of Basco Airport are also part of the package.Thailand looks to US for trade and defenceThailand is another major partner in the package. Trump and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul announced the substantial conclusion of negotiations on a reciprocal trade agreement that would eliminate tariffs on 99 percent of goods once signed.The proposed agreement also seeks to remove trade barriers affecting American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry.On the defence front, Thailand intends to spend up to $123 million on American-made High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems (HIMARS). If completed, the purchase could mark the first acquisition of the rocket artillery system by a country in mainland Southeast Asia, according to the White House.Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei join the energy and AI pushThe package also covers energy and technology investments in Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei. In Indonesia, US company Latitude Energy and sovereign wealth fund Danantara are negotiating a $2 billion project to improve the utilisation of the country's coal resources using American technology.In Malaysia, Navajo Transitional Energy Company has signed a three-year, $100 million agreement to supply coal from its Montana mine to TNB Fuel Services, a subsidiary of national power utility Tenaga Nasional Berhad. Malaysia will also work with a US consortium to develop sovereign AI cloud infrastructure, with Washington offering $50 million in support.In Brunei, Unified National Networks plans to award US company Vertiv a contract for the Rimba Data Centre project, with nearly $1 billion in spending expected to be sourced from American vendors.You use AI every day. articles.title: Faults not fixed in 90% of homes in government insulation scheme
articles.summary: People who signed up to a government insulation scheme have been struggling to get their damaged homes repaired.
articles.body:
More than 90% of homes fitted with faulty insulation under energy-saving government schemes have not yet had repairs completed to fix the botched work, a minister has said.

The government found almost all homes that had external wall insulation installed as part of two of the government's ECO schemes had defects that needed repairing.

Speaking to a committee of MPs on Wednesday, Energy Minister Martin McClusky said repair works had been completed at 2,227 out of the 24,600 homes impacted.

He said he was shocked by the extent of the failures and has assured affected households they would not be asked to pay to sort out these problems.

McClusky told MPs the insulation schemes "didn't have correct oversight".

Ofgem oversees the ECO schemes and alongside TrustMark, a government-backed consumer protection service, is responsible for auditing homes to identify faulty installations.

The government and its partners have known about significant levels of defective and unsafe insulation for years, with audits finding poor work in October 2024.

Ken Palfrey, a 66-year-old retired builder from Birmingham, is among the home owners waiting for repairs.

He had external wall insulation installed through the ECO programme in 2024.

He claims the installation was "botched", causing damage to his window sills and leading to damp and mould on his walls.

He said he complained and after some months an inspection concluded the insulation had been fitted incorrectly and he was told it had to be removed immediately.

Palfrey said for two years he had been on a "merry-go-round", spending "hundreds and hundreds of hours writing emails and complaining to people".

Earlier this month, TrustMark referred his case to the National Energy Foundation (NEF), a charity that has funding from energy suppliers to put right damaged homes where the installer has gone out of business.

"It's been an absolute nightmare," Palfrey said.

"Every day of my life, every time you look at the insulation, you're worried about it."

A TrustMark spokesperson said it was working to contact affected households and to fix "the unacceptable problems left by this faulty external wall insulation scheme".

"We're sorry for what Mr Palfrey has been through and have referred him to the National Energy Foundation which should be able to get his insulation put right," the spokesperson said.

Labour MP Bill Esterson, the chair of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, told the BBC he was seeking assurances that the victims "will be supported in a timely fashion".

But he said he was concerned that Ofgem, Great Britain's energy regulator, had "failed to identify whether work had been carried out or completed to a decent standard".

When asked if he had confidence in Ofgem at the committee, McClusky did not answer the question directly.

He said: "There's clearly been failures in the system. We're designing a system now."

He added Ofgem was a "very different organisation than it was a number of years ago".

A spokesperson for Ofgem said: "It is unacceptable that households have been left with substandard ECO4 work. Ofgem was not responsible for assuring the quality of installations."

The spokesperson said the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) "is responsible for the design and overall outcomes of ECO, and that Ofgem's role did not include assessing installation quality".

"Our role, set by government, is to administer the scheme and hold suppliers to account for meeting their obligations," the Ofgem spokesperson added.

"When serious quality problems emerged, we went beyond our core role to support affected households and help establish the scale of the problem."

The BBC has asked TrustMark for comment.

The two ECO schemes that have caused widespread issues are known as ECO4 and Great British Insulation Scheme (GBIS).

ECO4 was launched in 2022 and since then, more than 300,000 homes have had heat pumps, solar panels and insulation fitted under the £4bn scheme. It is closing in December.

GBIS - which opened in 2023 and has now closed - was more narrowly designed to help households lower their energy bills by installing cheap insulation.

The BBC has been reporting on the impact of faulty insulation installed under these schemes in recent years.

Fuel Poverty Action, a campaign group, argues that problems with faulty upgrades under a range of government energy efficiency schemes could be affecting as many as 100,000 homes.

"Ignoring the other defective measures is shockingly negligent, and is causing huge harm," said Jonathan Bean, policy lead at Fuel Poverty Action.

"Defective internal wall insulation causes major hidden damage, making it a ticking time bomb in homes.

"The government estimates that 29% of it is defective but chose not to include it in the Find and Fix process."

A spokesperson for DESNZ said: "We inherited the failing ECO4 scheme, which we ended after it clearly let families down.

"No household should have to pay to put the issues right and TrustMark is working to support those affected to ensure this is the case.

"Our Warm Homes Plan will overhaul the system to protect consumers and ensure failings are not repeated."

articles.title: North Northamptonshire Council announces more heating oil support
articles.summary: North Northamptonshire Council is encouraging eligible residents to apply for more support.
articles.body:
Households using heating oil as their main energy source are being offered more financial support by North Northamptonshire Council.

Residents can apply for a £250 voucher in emergency situations where low oil levels would put health, safety or basic living conditions at risk.

Heating oil is not protected by the Ofgem energy price cap, which means those reliant on it feel price increases faster than those on mains gas or electricity.

The Reform UK-led council encouraged residents to see if they were eligible for support online .

Heating oil prices have been volatile since the conflict between the US and Iran began in March.

The government announced a £53m support package in response to rising costs.

Rural areas, including parts of North Northamptonshire, are among the most affected, the council said.

Greg Wilcox, its executive member for communities and rural affairs, added: "We know that times are hard for many households and we want to do all we can to support as many residents as possible."

articles.title: Japanese researchers embedded wireless-charging coils in asphalt and ran a heavy vehicle over them for 100,000 five-ton wheel-load passes; the pavement and most coils showed no visible damage, but one coil beneath the wheel path recorded a drop in output power
articles.summary: Japanese researchers successfully tested wireless-charging coils embedded in asphalt, demonstrating their durability and efficiency under heavy traffic conditions, paving the way for electric vehicles to recharge on the go.
articles.body: Researchers in Japan are developing a technology that would enable electric vehicles to recharge as they drive. Potentially saving time and eliminating the need to pause at recharging stations. The technology uses power-transmitting coils embedded in roads and receiving coils inserted beneath vehicles. However, equipment must withstand the repeated pressure of heavy traffic without compromising its ability to transmit power. A 2023 study by researchers from Tokyo University of Science and Toa Road Corporation tested the durability of coils embedded in asphalt by subjecting them to a large-scale investigation to simulate 100,000 wheel passes over the experimental area. The test revealed there was almost no visible physical damage after multiple rotations, and electrical measurements recorded an output power of 46 kilowatts.How the wireless charging road system works The technology was named dynamic wireless power transfer (DWPT). The system uses electromagnetic fields to transfer electricity from transmitter coils embedded under a road to a receiver coil on the electric vehicle. When a vehicle equipped with a receiver passes over the charging zone, the section of the road with coils charges the vehicle without the need to plug into a socket or charging cable. This technology could mitigate two major issues faced by electric vehicle owners: range anxiety and long recharging times. As a vehicle will be able to pull power while moving on designated roads, such an automobile could use a smaller battery and fewer charging stations.But installing electrical gear under asphalt roadways is more challenging. Road surfaces are continuously subjected to the weight of wheels, temperature fluctuations, and other factors. The coils also need to remain electrically functional after being buried under the pavement. To determine this, the Japanese researchers used a methyl methacrylate (MMA) resin mixture that would hold and safeguard the gear. They installed eight transmitter coils at two sites on a designated circular for a pavement test drive, with some parts between and others beneath the path of a vehicle.Heavy vehicles put the embedded coils to the testThe durability test was performed at a pavement testing site operated by Japan's Pavement Research Team. A heavy-duty vehicle then moved around the circular test track in automated mode at 30 km/h, with positioning devices kept on track. The team monitored 100,000 wheel rotations, which is equivalent to a five-ton wheel load. This method was chosen to test whether repeated exposure to vehicles weighing heavily on the asphalt would erode the pavement or fry the coils buried in it. The team compared the pavement and the coil properties before and after the vehicle rotations.Findings indicated that there was no damage inflicted on the surface of the pavement or the coils that were inserted. Additionally, electrical performance remained consistent throughout the experimental locations. As reported in the paper, the eight uncased coils had at least 49 kW of output and at least 88% transmission efficiency after the test. The caseless coil that was placed in the surface layer beneath the wheel path showed greater deterioration. It experienced a drop in output power to 4.3 kilowatts and a transmission efficiency of 10.4%. However, it still provided 46.4 kilowatt output and 81.2% transmission efficiency. Researchers speculated that direct wheel loading may have caused the greater deterioration.What the findings mean for future roadsThe Japanese experiment shows that the MMA resin mixture can help coils maintain the same mechanical properties while preserving electrical performance. The researchers also observed that the installation location and cases had effects on durability. Coils below the binder layer or encased exhibited less degradation than coils directly below the wheel path.This might give future designers of wireless charging roads a glimpse of its shortcomings, where engineers will need to factor in traffic volume, wheel distribution, pavement depth, and protective casing. The prototype sent about 10 kilowatts to a car, providing 63.3% of the amount of electricity it used in the experiment; the underground coil remained stable after 18 months, while the 20 23 test looked at how long the coil buried in the asphalt would last.You use AI every day. articles.title: COP31 Presidency releases draft omitting fossil fuel transition plan
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: As the ongoing UN climate conference entered the last leg of negotiations to arrive at some outcome by consensus in Antalya, Turkiye, the COP31
articles.body: NEW DELHI: As the ongoing UN climate conference entered the last leg of negotiations to arrive at some outcome by consensus in Antalya, Turkiye, the COP31 Presidency on Thursday released a new draft text with certain compromises, where it doesn’t mention a point on transitioning away from fossil fuels and drops the explicit amount for tripling the adaptation finance figure.Though it recognises increasing electrification footprints under 35% electrification by 2035 plan and retains the ambition, the silence on fossil fuels may not go down well with countries demanding their gradual phase-down. The electrification goal, however, makes reference to the need for finance support and enabling energy access for people, but lacks measures to address these needs.The draft text in the current form appears to be an attempt to keep both fossil fuel user/exporter countries and the developed nations, who resisted a clear adaptation finance goal, on board while arriving at a final cover decision with consensus.The formulation of keeping mum on fossil fuel transition may suit India which has maintained that the use of fossil fuels (oil, gas and coal) remains the mainstay of the country’s economic growth agenda while it has voluntarily been moving away from them by increasing the footprints of renewable energy in a big way.On the other hand, India and other developing countries including China may not be pleased with what the Presidency did on the finance issue as the draft cover decision left the Global Goal on Adaptation without finance, even as there has been a demand for the tripling of adaptation finance.“Erasing explicit calls to transition away from fossil fuels and dropping the COP30 fossil fuel roadmap in the draft is a glaring regression. You cannot solve a fossil fuel crisis by pretending we don’t need to phase out fossil fuels... Dropping the explicit $120 billion adaptation finance figure, Oxfam’s grant-equivalent baseline, and debt-pause protections from the draft is a regressive retreat that leaves debt-burdened nations to shoulder adaptation costs on their own,” said Harjeet Singh, a climate expert, who has been following the negotiation at COP31.“The proposed new electrification goal doesn’t even aim to reduce fossil fuel use, encourage renewables or meet the needs of the hundreds of millions of people who currently lack energy access. Instead, there is a risk that data centres, with their exploding energy demand, will take advantage of the electrification goal as it currently stands," said Teresa Anderson, global lead on climate justice at ActionAid International.You use AI every day. articles.title: Susan Smith denied parole again 32 years after drowning her two sons
articles.summary: At a hearing on the possibility of parole, Smith said she wished she could change the past, and her two children "did not deserve to die".
articles.body:
A South Carolina woman who admitted to drowning her two sons 32 years ago has been denied parole for a second time.

Susan Smith, 55, was convicted of killing her boys by strapping them into their car seats and rolling her vehicle into a lake in 1994.

"I got to my lowest when I let that car go into that lake," Smith said during a hearing on Thursday with the state board that decides whether to release those in prison on parole.

The seven-member board later unanimously turned down her request to be freed. The father of the two boys has vowed to continue to oppose her release, and several people spoke against her in the hearing.

Smith, whose lawyers had argued she suffered a mental breakdown during the crime, can apply to the South Carolina Board of Probation, Parole and Pardon Services for parole every two years.

She told the board that she had changed and matured since killing three-year-old Michael and one-year-old Alex, and that "I am not the same person I was 32 years ago".

She also said she was "very, very sorry" and that she would go back and change the circumstances if she could.

"They were innocent children," Smith said. "They did not deserve to die."

Her children's father, David Smith, attended the hearing so he could advocate for their sons, he said.

The 32 years, he said, do not take away what Smith "deliberately" did.

"I know in my heart granting her parole would be a huge injustice to Michael and Alex," said David Smith, who had pinned a photo of both his sons to his lapel.

Prosecutors argued during the trial that Smith killed the boys after a man with whom she was having an affair told her that her sons were the reason that the pair did not have a future together.

At Thursday's hearing, Smith said: "This did not happen because of a man. That's just not true."

When the boys first disappeared, Smith said she was carjacked late at night and a man drove away with her car. While she pleaded publicly for their safe return, her sons were at the bottom of a nearby lake.

But ultimately she confessed to the crime.

Defence lawyers said she had wanted to die with her children but left the car at the last minute.

Smith was convicted of murder. Under South Carolina law at the time, she was allowed to request parole every two years after serving 30 years in prison.

In the US, some people convicted of crimes are eligible for parole, which means they can be released from incarceration.

She would have needed two-thirds of the board members present to vote in her favour to be freed.

articles.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
articles.summary: The unprecedented International Court of Justice verdict concerns a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands.
articles.body:
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.

Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.

A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.

Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications

The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.

The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.

After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.

Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.

The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.

Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.

He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.

Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.

While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.

Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.

In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.

The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.

It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.

The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.

"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."

Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".

Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".

To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.

Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.

Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.

Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".

He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.

However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.

The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.

Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.

He added that, while ruling against Myanmar did not mean the court would find similarly with Gaza, if it had not found Myanmar responsible, the case against Israel "would, in effect, be over". Israel says the case against it is "wholly unfounded".

Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, told the BBC that the court had not accepted Myanmar's counter-terrorism defence and had found for the first time that rape and sexual violence was an act of genocide, positions it would bear in mind for future cases.

A spokesperson for the US State Department said "the proper interpretation" of the Genocide Convention is of "paramount importance", and so is "preventing politicisation" of the International Criminal Court. "We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," they said.

They said they share the "grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups", and added the US is the "leading donor for the Rohingya refugee humanitarian response".

Following Thursday's ruling, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was ordering Myanmar's defence attaché be expelled and that he was summoning its charge d'affaires.

He pledged to set out "further action in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held to account" after a cross-party group of MPs called for the government to resume sanctions against Myanmar's military.

articles.title: New York's Governors Island has unveiled a giant oyster-inspired public artwork that is also an outdoor amphitheatre; artist Alan Michelson's installation explores the island's Indigenous and maritime history
articles.summary: New York's Governors Island has unveiled a large oyster-inspired public artwork that brings together sculpture, history and environmental restoration.
articles.body: New York's Governors Island has unveiled a large oyster-inspired public artwork that brings together sculpture, history and environmental restoration. Created by Mohawk artist Alan Michelson, the installation, titled The Oyster, transforms part of the island's waterfront into an outdoor amphitheatre where visitors can gather and explore the region's Indigenous past. Located along the Western Promenade, the artwork draws attention to the historical importance of oysters in New York Harbor and the relationship between Indigenous communities and the surrounding waters.The giant oyster-inspired artwork reflect Governors Island's Indigenous historyThe Oyster is a monumental outdoor sculpture commissioned by More Art in partnership with Billion Oyster Project and co-presented by Governors Island Arts. According to More Art, the installation opened to the public on July 30, 2026, and is scheduled to remain on view until November 30, 2026.The artwork takes inspiration from pre-colonial Lenape oyster middens, which were large accumulations of oyster shells created over generations. These formations provide evidence of the Indigenous communities that lived in the region and their longstanding relationship with the natural resources of New York Harbor.Oysters were an important part of Lenape culture, and their shells reflected more than a source of food. As explained in More Art's land acknowledgement, the middens represented generations of connections between Indigenous communities and the harbour's natural abundance. These relationships were significantly disrupted by colonisation.Michelson's installation brings attention to this history by using the oyster as a symbol of both cultural heritage and environmental importance.The sculpture combines art with the function of an outdoor amphitheatreUnlike a conventional sculpture designed primarily for viewing, The Oyster has been created as a space where people can gather. Its structure functions partly as a landform and partly as an amphitheatre, allowing visitors to sit within and around the installation.According to the Governors Island public art description, the artwork stands on the island's western shore, facing New York Harbor and the Statue of Liberty. Its position gives visitors an opportunity to experience the installation alongside the waterfront landscape that forms an important part of its subject.The design also draws inspiration from Indigenous geoglyphs and shaped shell middens. Rather than simply recreating an oyster or a natural reef, Michelson has developed a structure that connects historical land formations with contemporary public art. The installation is intended to serve as a gathering place as well as a memorial to the region's changing relationship with its natural environment.How were recycled oyster shells incorporated into the installationThe construction of The Oyster reflects the environmental message behind the artwork. Developed in partnership with Billion Oyster Project, the installation uses salvaged oyster shells and steel mesh gabions, drawing on techniques associated with reef construction and restoration.Governors Island's official description explains that the structure uses these materials to function simultaneously as a habitat, monument and public gathering space. Gabions are mesh containers that hold materials such as stones or shells together, making them useful in building structures inspired by natural reef formations.This approach connects the artwork to the work of Billion Oyster Project, a nonprofit organisation focused on restoring oyster reefs in New York Harbor. According to More Art, the organisation has restored more than 150 million oysters across nearly 18 acres of reef and recycled over 3 million pounds of oyster shells collected from New York City restaurants.More Art also states that some elements of the sculpture will be returned to New York Harbor after the exhibition ends. These materials will become part of local reef restoration efforts.The artwork brings community voices into its designAnother distinctive feature of The Oyster is the large-scale text installation surrounding the sculpture. Painted directly onto the ground in purple and white, the text brings together reflections on oysters from literature, history, ecology and popular culture.The project also includes contributions from students at New York Harbor School and members of the Governors Island community. Their participation gives the installation a wider perspective, connecting the artwork with people who live, study and spend time around the harbour.The colours used in the text installation carry historical meaning as well. According to More Art, the purple and white palette references wampum, shell beads historically used by the Lenape and other Eastern Woodlands nations in sacred cultural exchanges. Wampum played a role in exchange, diplomacy and record-keeping.Governors Island has listed boat tours, walking performances, conversations and commissioned works among the programmes designed to bring visitors together around the sculpture. Free guided tours are scheduled for Saturdays and Sundays at noon and 4 pm.Alan Michelson's work explores histories often overlooked in public spacesThe Oyster is part of More Art's 2026 initiative, Reframing 1776: Land, Water, and the Work of Repair. The programme brings together artistic projects that respond to the United States' 250th anniversary through Indigenous perspectives and environmental histories.Michelson, a New York-based Mohawk artist and member of Six Nations of the Grand River, has spent more than 3 decades creating sculptures, videos, installations and public artworks that explore place, memory and overlooked histories.More Art notes that his previous public commissions include The Knowledge Keepers at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston and Mantle, a permanent monument honouring Virginia's Native nations at the Virginia State Capitol in Richmond.His work has also been included in the collections of the Whitney Museum of American Art, the Smithsonian American Art Museum and the National Gallery of Canada.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Canada has declared a reward of up to $250,000 for information leading to the arrest of Satinderjeet Singh aka Goldy Brar, after naming him the number-one suspect on the Bolo Program’s new Top 25 list of Canada’s most wanted fugitives.Brar, who is also on the US top ten list, is the first Indian origin gangster to make it to the top of both lists, sources said. The development also indicates Brar may have slipped into Canada after FBI's Op Hardball, alerting the Canadian authorities.Announced Thursday by the Winnipeg Police Service, the reward applies to tips leading to the 32-year-old’s arrest in either Canada or the United States and remains active until November 2, 2027.Brar is wanted on a Canada-wide warrant for first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder in connection with the September 20, 2023, fatal shooting of 39-year-old Sukhdool Singh Gill alias Sukha Duneke at a residence on Hazelton Drive in northwest Winnipeg.Following an extensive multi-agency investigation involving the Homicide Unit, the RCMP, and Manitoba Justice, arrest warrants were authorized on February 23, 2026, for both Brar and a second suspect, 26-year-old Karanbir Singh, who faces identical charges. Both men remain at large.The coordinated push across North America follows major US federal action earlier this year. On July 7, the US Attorney’s Office unsealed indictments from Operation Hard Ball linking Brar to the Lawrence Bishnoi Organized Crime Group and the murder of a prominent Indian figure in British Columbia.Op Hardball had also indicted Brar and Lawrence Bishnoi for orchestrating the killing of 'HSN' (short for Nijjar), reframing the high-profile assassination as a gangland hit rather than a state-sponsored killing. He was subsequently added to the FBI’s Top 10 Most Wanted Fugitives list with a $1 million U.S. reward.“We will aggressively defend our cities, and our country, against this kind of violence,” said Winnipeg Deputy Chief Cam Mackid in a statement. “We don’t accept it, and we will be relentless.”Authorities warned that both suspects are considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached. articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin said I "believe our response will be far more painful than what the Kyiv regime did" to the Kerch Strait bridge this week.
articles.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed Thursday to respond to Ukraine in a "far more painful" manner after Volodymyr Zelenskyy's forces heavily damaged the Kerch Strait bridge that has become a symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea. The warning was issued as Ukraine's president said he arrived in Berlin, Germany for talks with more than 40 partners aimed at ending the war, including with President Donald Trump's son-in-law and advisor Jared Kushner and U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff. "We will respond to these strikes. And I want everyone to know this: I believe our response will be far more painful than what the Kyiv regime did to the bridge," Putin said after meeting with President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping for trilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, China, according to Reuters. "We will, of course, restore the bridge. The road section suffered serious damage," Putin reportedly added. UKRAINE RELEASE VIDEO SHOWING DAMAGE PUTIN'S PRIZE BRIDGE FOLLOWING 'UNPRECEDENTED OPERATION' IN CRIMEA Ukraine attacked the bridge for the third time this week prior to Putin making his remarks, Reuters reported. A Russian official told The Associated Press that the latest strike on the bridge linking Russia to Crimea halted rail traffic. On Tuesday, the Security Service of Ukraine released videos showing the aftermath of a drone strike on the bridge, which destroyed one of its two arches and a roadway underneath it. Putin said Thursday that he discussed with Russia's Security Council a potential stoppage of attacks at sea and against energy facilities, and "asked everyone to give it further thought and come back to it, hoping that perhaps some kind of agreement could be reached," according to Reuters. "But after the strikes on the Crimean Bridge, there will be no agreements," Putin added. TRUMP HISTORIC SUMMIT XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE Zelenskyy has described the bridge as the "main military crossing from Russian territory into our Ukrainian Crimea." Ahead of Thursday's Coalition of the Willing meeting in Germany, Zelenskyy said "Ukraine’s priorities are strengthening our air defense, energy and financial support, the diplomatic track, and the next steps toward ending the war and guaranteeing security. "Bilateral meetings with European partners are also planned, and, of course, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz. There will also be a format involving the American side and European national security advisors," he added. Kushner said on X that the U.S. priorities for the trip "are to further strengthen our close coordination with Ukraine and Europe, work toward a unified position on the key elements of a lasting peace, and to jointly prepare the agenda and proposed format for the next round of multilateral negotiations." articles.title: Pannun case: Indian national Nikhil Gupta to be sentenced on Friday in murder-for-hire plot
articles.summary: Indian national Nikhil Gupta, accused of plotting to assassinate Khalistani separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun on American soil, is set to be sentenced by
articles.body: Indian national Nikhil Gupta, accused of plotting to assassinate Khalistani separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun on American soil, is set to be sentenced by a US federal court on Friday. Prosecutors have sought a 24-year prison term, arguing that his role in the murder-for-hire plot was serious and warranted a stringent punishment.Gupta, 55, is scheduled to be sentenced at around 10 am local time on November 20 by US District Judge Victor Marrero in the Southern District of New York.He pleaded guilty earlier this year to three charges: murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering. The charges stem from his alleged involvement in a plot to kill Pannun, who holds American and Canadian citizenship, in New York.US prosecutors seek 24-year sentenceIn a 20-page submission to the court last week, US prosecutors sought a sentence of 293 months (about 24 years and five months) in prison for Gupta, according to news agency PTI.US Attorney James McDonald described Gupta's conduct as "as brutal as it was brazen" and said he played a crucial role in a foreign plot to kill an American citizen on US soil."He was a crucial participant in a foreign plot to execute a US citizen on US soil. The Court should impose a sentence that reflects the magnitude of the crime and sends a message that the violent silencing of voices in this country will not be tolerated," McDonald said.The prosecution argued that Gupta and his co-conspirators, "including at least one Indian Government employee", plotted to kill an American citizen because of the victim's political ideology.Calling it "a crime of the utmost seriousness", the government said a sentence at the higher end of the US Sentencing Guidelines was necessary."The Government submits that a sentence at the top of the United States Sentencing Guidelines range of 235 to 293 months' incarceration is necessary to serve the legitimate purposes of sentencing," the submission said.Gupta seeks reduced sentenceGupta's lawyers have urged the court to impose a significantly shorter sentence, backing the Probation Department's recommendation of 144 months (12 years) in prison, followed by three years of supervised release.According to his defence team, the Probation Department calculated an advisory sentencing range of 235 to 293 months but recommended a substantial reduction after considering Gupta's personal circumstances and the details of the case.His lawyers said the recommendation reflected the assessment of the probation officer, who had interviewed Gupta, reviewed the investigative record and considered the relevant sentencing factors.They pointed out that Gupta had no prior criminal record and was suffering from untreated alcohol dependence when the offence took place.They also argued that a lengthy prison term would carry significant consequences for the 55-year-old. "Gupta does not minimise" the seriousness of his actions, his lawyers said."He agreed to arrange the murder of another person, and that conduct warrants a term of imprisonment. But the sentence this Court imposes should be sufficient, and not greater than necessary, to serve the purposes of sentencing as to this defendant," they submitted.According to the indictment, other public court documents and statements made in court, Gupta allegedly worked with several individuals in India and elsewhere in 2023 to arrange Pannun's assassination. The alleged plot involved Vikash Yadav, a co-defendant whom Gupta was working with at the time.At Yadav's direction, Gupta contacted an individual he believed to be associated with criminal networks and sought his help in arranging a hitman to kill Pannun in New York City. However, the individual was actually a confidential source working with the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), PTI reported.Gupta was arrested in the Czech Republic on June 30, 2023, and later extradited to the United States.The 54-year-old Indian national has pleaded guilty to charges including murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. The offences carry maximum sentences of 10 years, 10 years, and 20 years in prison, respectively.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
